title: When would you deliberately accept data loss — and why is the answer "when the data is reconstructable or low-value enough that guaranteeing durability would cost more than losing it" (telemetry, derived analytics, temporary caches vs financial transactions, ownership records) — and why must you define the acceptable loss window explicitly rather than treating every byte as equally critical?
shortTitle: When would you deliberately accept data loss, and why must you define the loss window explicitly?

s1_definition.profdef: Durability guarantees are not free — synchronous replication, fsync-on-every-write, and acknowledged persistence cost latency, throughput, and money, so you deliberately accept data loss for data whose value is lower than the cost of guaranteeing it. Data that is reconstructable (derived analytics you can recompute), regenerable (temporary caches), or inherently low-stakes and high-volume (telemetry, metrics) can tolerate loss, whereas financial transactions and ownership records must never be lost. The acceptable loss window — how much data, over what time, you are willing to lose — must be stated explicitly per data class, because treating every byte as equally critical forces the cheapest, most replaceable data to pay the same expensive durability tax as the most critical data, which is both wasteful and, by overloading the durable path, can actually endanger the critical data.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India keeps two very different kinds of records. The ledger of who owns how much money must survive fire, flood, and power failure — it is copied to multiple vaults and confirmed before anyone walks away. But the scribbled tally of how many customers walked in each hour is just a convenience; if a page blows away, the bank shrugs, because that number can be estimated again and losing it costs nothing. The mistake would be to treat the hourly tally with the same fireproof-vault ceremony as the ledger — it would waste effort and slow down the one thing that truly matters. So the bank decides, in advance and in writing, exactly how much of each kind of record it can afford to lose.
s1_definition.oneliner: Accept data loss where the data is reconstructable or low-value enough that durability would cost more than the loss, and write down the acceptable loss window per data class so the cheap data never taxes the critical data.

**Professional definition:** Durability guarantees are not free — synchronous replication, fsync-on-every-write, and acknowledged persistence cost latency, throughput, and money, so you deliberately accept data loss for data whose value is lower than the cost of guaranteeing it. Data that is reconstructable (derived analytics you can recompute), regenerable (temporary caches), or inherently low-stakes and high-volume (telemetry, metrics) can tolerate loss, whereas financial transactions and ownership records must never be lost. The acceptable loss window — how much data, over what time, you are willing to lose — must be stated explicitly per data class, because treating every byte as equally critical forces the cheapest, most replaceable data to pay the same expensive durability tax as the most critical data, which is both wasteful and, by overloading the durable path, can actually endanger the critical data.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India keeps two very different kinds of records. The ledger of who owns how much money must survive fire, flood, and power failure — it is copied to multiple vaults and confirmed before anyone walks away. But the scribbled tally of how many customers walked in each hour is just a convenience; if a page blows away, the bank shrugs, because that number can be estimated again and losing it costs nothing. The mistake would be to treat the hourly tally with the same fireproof-vault ceremony as the ledger — it would waste effort and slow down the one thing that truly matters. So the bank decides, in advance and in writing, exactly how much of each kind of record it can afford to lose.

**One line to remember:** Accept data loss where the data is reconstructable or low-value enough that durability would cost more than the loss, and write down the acceptable loss window per data class so the cheap data never taxes the critical data.

sections.s2_technical:
Durability is a spectrum with a price at every level. At the strong end, a write is not acknowledged until it is persisted to disk and replicated synchronously to other nodes, which maximises safety but adds latency and limits throughput. At the weak end, a write is acknowledged immediately and flushed to disk or replicated later, which is fast and cheap but can lose recent writes if the node crashes before the flush. Every system chooses a point on this spectrum, and the right point depends entirely on the value of the data.

The decision rule is a comparison of two costs: the cost of guaranteeing durability versus the cost of losing the data. For financial transactions and ownership records, the cost of loss is catastrophic — lost money, legal liability, regulatory breach — so you pay for strong durability no matter the price. For telemetry, metrics, and request logs, the cost of losing a few seconds of data is near zero because the data is high-volume and individually unimportant, and you are sampling trends anyway, so cheap, lossy, high-throughput paths are correct. For derived analytics and materialised views, the data is reconstructable by recomputing from the source of truth, so losing it costs only the recomputation, not the information. For temporary caches, the data is regenerable from the primary store on the next miss, so loss costs only a cache-miss, not correctness.

This is why you classify data rather than treating it uniformly. If you apply the ledger's strong-durability path to telemetry, you force a massive volume of low-value writes through your most expensive, most contended pipeline. That is wasteful, and worse, it is dangerous: the telemetry flood can saturate the durable write path and the replication link, adding latency and risk to the financial transactions that actually need that path. So mixing the cheap and the critical on the same strong-durability path can endanger the critical data. Separating data classes onto appropriately-durable paths protects the critical class.

Defining the acceptable loss window explicitly is the discipline that makes this safe and operable. For each data class you state a Recovery Point Objective — the maximum amount of data, measured in time, you are willing to lose in a failure. For the ledger it is zero: no committed transaction may ever be lost, which dictates synchronous replication and acknowledged commits. For telemetry it might be sixty seconds: losing up to a minute of metrics on a crash is acceptable, which permits buffering and asynchronous flushes. For a cache it is effectively total: the entire cache may be lost at any time with only a performance impact. Writing these windows down turns durability from a vague aspiration into concrete engineering choices — replication mode, flush frequency, acknowledgement policy, buffer sizes — and it makes the trade-offs auditable, which matters in a regulated bank.

The senior nuance is that the loss window must match the mechanism, and the mechanism must be tested. Claiming a sixty-second telemetry window while actually buffering five minutes in memory means a crash loses five minutes, not sixty seconds, so the stated window is a lie until verified. And the critical-data window of zero must be proven by testing crashes in the exact window between a client acknowledgement and the durable commit, because that is where silent loss hides. So I pair each explicit loss window with a failure-injection test that proves the system actually honors it — the ledger loses nothing on a mid-commit crash, and telemetry loses no more than its stated window.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India one pipeline handles both transfer records and click telemetry, and the team originally pushed both through the same strong-durability path.

Problem 1 — the telemetry volume is a hundred times the transfer volume, and forcing it through synchronous replication saturated the durable path, adding latency to actual transfers. This is exactly why cheap data must not share the critical data's durability path, and why mixing them endangers the critical class.

Problem 2 — nobody had written down an acceptable loss window, so engineers argued about whether telemetry needed replication at all. Defining it explicitly — transfers zero loss, telemetry up to sixty seconds, cache total — settled the design. This is exactly why the loss window must be explicit per data class.

Problem 3 — a crash test revealed telemetry was buffered in memory for five minutes, violating the stated sixty-second window. This is exactly why the window must match the mechanism and be verified by failure injection.

The demo routes three data classes — transfers, telemetry, cache — through durability policies matched to their loss windows, simulates a crash, and reports what each class lost, proving transfers lose nothing while telemetry loses only within its window.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is three streams: five transfer records (critical, loss window zero), twenty-three telemetry clicks (low value, loss window sixty seconds, buffer flushed every ten), and a cache (regenerable, total loss acceptable).

Step 1: Each transfer is written to the durable sink, which persists and conceptually replicates it before acknowledging. By the time the write call returns, the transfer is safe, so an acknowledged transfer cannot be lost.

Step 2: Each telemetry click is appended to the buffered sink and acknowledged immediately, which is fast. Every time the buffer reaches ten, it is flushed to durable storage. After twenty-three clicks, two full batches of ten have been flushed (twenty survived) and three remain in the unflushed buffer.

Step 3: A crash is simulated at this exact moment. The durable sink holds all five transfers because each was acknowledged only after being made durable, so transfers lose nothing, honoring the zero-loss window.

Step 4: The buffered sink loses only its three unflushed clicks, because the flushed twenty are durable. Three lost clicks is well within the sixty-second window, because the buffer was deliberately sized so its contents never represent more than sixty seconds of data — the window matches the mechanism.

Step 5: The cache is simply gone, which is acceptable because it is regenerated from the source of truth on the next miss, so correctness is intact and only performance is briefly affected. The demo reports each class against its stated window, proving the critical data lost nothing while the cheap data lost only within its explicitly accepted window.

```
2026-10-24 18:50:10 [INFO] === Durability matched to data value (explicit loss windows) ===
2026-10-24 18:50:10 [SEVERE] *** CRASH ***
2026-10-24 18:50:10 [INFO] Transfers (RPO=0s): survived=5 lost=0 zero loss
2026-10-24 18:50:10 [INFO] Telemetry (RPO=60s): survived=20 lost=3 within window
2026-10-24 18:50:10 [INFO] Cache (VOLATILE): lost entirely — regenerated on next miss, correctness intact
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
I would deliberately accept data loss when the data is reconstructable or low-value enough that guaranteeing its durability would cost more than losing it. Durability is not free — synchronous replication, flushing to disk on every write, and acknowledged persistence all cost latency, throughput, and money. So the decision is a comparison of two costs: the cost of guaranteeing durability versus the cost of losing the data. For financial transactions and ownership records the cost of loss is catastrophic, so I pay for strong durability regardless of price. For telemetry, metrics, derived analytics, and temporary caches, the cost of losing a little recent data is near zero, so a cheap, fast, lossy path is the correct engineering choice.

The reason this matters is that the data classes are genuinely different. Telemetry and metrics are high-volume and individually unimportant — you are tracking trends, so losing a few seconds changes nothing. Derived analytics and materialised views are reconstructable by recomputing from the source of truth, so losing them costs only the recomputation. Caches are regenerable from the primary store on the next miss, so loss costs a cache-miss, not correctness. But a transfer or an ownership record cannot be recreated once lost, so it must never be lost. Treating all of these as equally critical is the mistake.

And it is not just wasteful to over-protect cheap data — it is actively dangerous. If I force a hundred-to-one volume of telemetry through the same strong-durability pipeline that transfers depend on, the telemetry flood can saturate the durable write path and the replication link, adding latency and risk to the very transactions that need that path most. So mixing the cheap and the critical on one durable path can endanger the critical class. Separating them onto appropriately-durable paths is what protects the money.

This is exactly why the acceptable loss window must be explicit per data class rather than left vague. For each class I state a Recovery Point Objective — the maximum data, measured in time, I am willing to lose. For the ledger it is zero, which dictates synchronous replication and acknowledging a commit only after it is durable. For telemetry it might be sixty seconds, which permits buffering and asynchronous flushes. For a cache it is total. Writing these down turns durability from a vague wish into concrete choices about replication mode, flush frequency, and acknowledgement policy, and in a regulated bank it makes those trade-offs auditable. The senior point I always add is that the window must match the mechanism and be tested — claiming a sixty-second telemetry window while actually buffering five minutes in memory is a lie until you prove it, and a zero-loss claim for transfers must be verified by crashing the system in the exact window between the acknowledgement and the durable commit.

In my banking work this came straight from a real problem: transfers and click telemetry shared one strong-durability pipeline, and the telemetry volume saturated it and delayed actual transfers. We classified the data, wrote down the loss windows — transfers zero, telemetry sixty seconds, cache total — and routed each class to a path that matched its window, with the critical transfers fully isolated from the telemetry flood. A crash test even caught that telemetry was buffered far longer than its stated window, which we fixed by sizing the buffer to the window. The result was that transfers were provably never lost, telemetry lost only within its explicitly accepted window, and the cache could vanish harmlessly — each byte protected exactly as much as its value deserved, and no more.

keyPoints: Database per service: each microservice owns its data
Idempotency: same request produces same result — safe retries
Eventual consistency: services sync via events, not distributed locks
Shared database anti-pattern: breaks service independence
